title: Supplements: What You Actually Need (and What to Skip)
excerpt: The supplement aisle is worth more than the food it claims to replace. Here's an evidence-based guide to which supplements Indians commonly need — and how to check before buying.
keywords: which supplements do I need, vitamin D deficiency India, B12 supplement, supplements guide, supplements to avoid
author: Dietitian Tejal
quickAnswer: Most healthy people eating a balanced Indian diet do not need a shelf of supplements — but a few are genuinely common: vitamin D (deficiency is widespread in India — test first), B12 (vegetarians and vegans are at risk — test), iron (women, if anaemic — test), and folic acid (pregnancy, prescribed). The rule: test before supplementing, buy third-party-tested brands, and never treat supplements as a substitute for food.

sections.heading: Why is the supplement aisle so confusing?
sections.body:
Supplements are a massive market built on anxiety and aspirational health — 'immunity', 'energy', 'detox', 'performance'. Most products have weak or no evidence for their claims, and regulation of claims is looser than for medicines.
The reality: your body needs nutrients, and it prefers them from food, where they come with fibre and other compounds. Supplements matter when there is a genuine deficiency or a specific need — and those are found by testing, not by browsing.

sections.heading: Which deficiencies are common in India?
sections.body:
Vitamin D tops the list — widespread deficiency because of indoor lifestyles, clothing and skin pigmentation; a blood test is the only way to know your level. B12 is common in vegetarians and vegans, and in people on long-term acid-reducer medication. Iron deficiency is common in women and children (anaemia is a major Indian health issue).
Each is tested easily and treated simply — but the dose and form matter, and self-supplementing iron or B12 without knowing the level wastes money and can be unsafe (especially iron for men and post-menopausal women).

sections.heading: When are supplements genuinely needed?
sections.body:
Pregnancy (folic acid, often iron, calcium, vitamin D and DHA — prescribed), diagnosed deficiency (vitamin D, B12, iron), restrictive diets (vegans need B12; vegans and some vegetarians may need iron, calcium, iodine), medical conditions affecting absorption, and older adults (vitamin D, often B12 and calcium).
Athletes may need targeted support (creatine, protein powder, electrolytes) based on their sport — that is sport-specific, not 'everyone needs this'. The common thread: a specific reason, guided by tests or a professional.

sections.heading: How do you choose a safe supplement?
sections.body:
Look for third-party testing (NSF, USP, or an equivalent certification), a supplement facts panel that lists exact doses, no 'proprietary blend' hiding ingredients, and no miracle claims. Indian brands vary widely — certification matters.
Avoid megadoses (more than 100% of daily needs without a medical reason), 'immune-boosting' mystery blends, and anything sold with a 'cure' claim. If a product promises what medicine cannot, it is not medicine — it is marketing.

sections.heading: How do supplements and food work together?
sections.body:
Supplements fill gaps; food builds the pattern. A multivitamin does not rescue a diet of junk — it is a rounding tool at best, and high-dose isolated nutrients can even interfere with absorption of others (iron with calcium, for example).
The practical order: fix the food pattern first, test the likely gaps, supplement what is genuinely low, and re-test after treatment. This approach costs less, works better and avoids the side effects of unnecessary pills. Your doctor and dietitian can run the whole sequence with you.

faqs.question: Should everyone take a multivitamin?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — a balanced diet covers most needs. Multivitamins are reasonable for some groups (older adults, restrictive diets, poor appetite) but are not a substitute for food and not universally needed.

faqs.question: Can I take vitamin D without testing?
faqs.answer: A short, low-dose course is common in India given the prevalence, but proper treatment needs a level — the dose to correct deficiency differs from maintenance. Test once, then follow your doctor's plan.

faqs.question: Are herbal supplements safe?
faqs.answer: Not automatically — 'natural' does not mean safe. Herbal products can interact with medicines and cause liver injury. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including herbs.

faqs.question: Do protein powders count as supplements?
faqs.answer: Yes — and they are only needed when food cannot hit protein targets (athletes, recovery, some weight-loss plans). Choose a tested brand with minimal added sugar; it is food supplementing, not a drug.

title: Reading Nutrition Claims: 'Healthy', 'Natural' and 'Zero' Decoded
excerpt: Every packet has a story — and most are fiction. How to decode marketing claims on Indian packaged food so you are never fooled again.
keywords: food marketing claims, natural food claim, zero sugar label, healthy food claims India, decode food labels
author: Dietitian Tejal
quickAnswer: Marketing claims are regulated but permissive: 'natural' says almost nothing, 'zero added sugar' still allows fruit sugars and carbs, 'light' means reduced relative to the original (which may still be heavy), and 'healthy' is unregulated. The decoding rule: ignore the front of the packet, read the back — per-100g sugar, sodium, saturated fat, and the ingredient list. A claim is a hint to read the label, not a verdict.

sections.heading: Why do food packages lie (legally)?
sections.body:
The front of a packet is advertising; the nutrition panel is information. Regulators like FSSAI set rules for claims, but the rules are permissive — 'natural', 'no added colours', 'premium' and even 'healthy' can be used in ways that mislead without breaking them.
The result: 'digestive biscuits' that are mostly maida and sugar, 'fruit juices' that are largely water and sugar, 'protein snacks' that are sugar bombs. The marketing works — which is why decoding claims is a life skill.

sections.heading: What does 'natural' actually mean?
sections.body:
Almost nothing. 'Natural' is not a defined nutritional term — it does not mean low calorie, low sugar, organic, or healthy. A 'natural' snack can be fried, salted and sugary.
'No added colours' and 'no preservatives' say what is absent, not what is present — a product can be free of preservatives and full of sugar and maida. Judge by the nutrition panel, not the adjectives.

sections.heading: What does 'zero' or 'sugar-free' mean?
sections.body:
'No added sugar' means no sugar was added in processing — the product can still contain natural sugars (fruit, honey, milk) or refined carbs. 'Sugar-free' in the legal sense means under a tiny threshold per serving, which may still use sweeteners.
For diabetes and weight, the practical question is total carbohydrate and total sugar per 100g — not the sugar-free sticker. Many 'sugar-free' biscuits are still refined-flour and fat-dense and raise blood sugar.

sections.heading: How do you decode 'light', 'diet' and 'healthy'?
sections.body:
'Light' or 'lite' means reduced relative to the brand's original — the original may itself be heavy, and the light version may be high in sugar to compensate. 'Diet' has specific legal meanings for some products (like diet soft drinks) but is vague on food. 'Healthy' is effectively unregulated as a front-of-pack word.
The reliable approach: compare per-100g numbers with the regular version, and with a whole-food alternative. A plain apple beats every 'healthy' packaged snack, on every metric that matters.

sections.heading: What is the final decoding checklist?
sections.body:
Three numbers from the back of the packet: total sugar per 100g (over 22.5g = high), sodium (over 1.5g = high), saturated fat (over 5g = high). Then the ingredient list — the first three ingredients are the product. Then the serving size — multiply by what you actually eat.
And the meta-rule: the more claims on the front, the more carefully you should read the back. Foods that need no marketing are usually the foods worth buying.

faqs.question: Is 'no added sugar' the same as sugar-free?
faqs.answer: No — 'no added sugar' means none was added during processing, but natural sugars may remain. 'Sugar-free' legally means negligible sugar per serving, but often with sweeteners and carbs. Check total carbs and sugar.

faqs.question: Are 'digestive' biscuits good for digestion?
faqs.answer: No more than any biscuit — the name is marketing. Most are refined flour, sugar and palm oil with a little bran. If you want fibre, eat oats, dal or fruit instead.

faqs.question: Is '100% fruit juice' healthy?
faqs.answer: It has vitamins but also the sugar of several fruits without the fibre — it behaves like a sugary drink for blood sugar. Whole fruit is the better choice; juice is an occasional small treat.

faqs.question: Can I trust 'FSSAI approved' on the front?
faqs.answer: FSSAI approval is a safety baseline every legal product has — it is not a health endorsement. 'FSSAI approved' on the front is marketing dressing; the nutrition panel remains the truth.

title: How DietFiniti's Weight-Loss Program Actually Works
excerpt: Before you sign up, know exactly how the program runs: the form, the plan, weekly reviews, and what you can realistically expect from us — and from yourself.
keywords: DietFiniti program, weight loss program Mumbai, how DietFiniti works, dietitian program India, weekly diet plan
author: Dietitian Tejal
quickAnswer: DietFiniti's program runs in a clear loop: book and pay, fill a detailed history form (health, medications, routine, food preferences), get assigned a dietitian and counsellor, receive a personalised plan built around Indian food, update progress weekly, and receive plan adjustments. It works online anywhere in India or at our Lower Parel and Thane clinics. We are explicit about what we do not do: no medicines, no powders, no guaranteed numbers.

sections.heading: What happens after you book?
sections.body:
You book through the website or WhatsApp and complete the payment. Then comes the foundation of everything: a detailed history form covering your goals, health conditions, medications, allergies, work and sleep routine, cooking setup and food preferences.
This form is why the plan works — it converts a general diet into a personal one. A hostel student, a shift-working nurse and a home cook with diabetes get different plans even for the same goal, because their days are different.

sections.heading: What does the weekly rhythm look like?
sections.body:
You update progress every week — weight, meals, challenges, how the plan felt — and the plan is revised based on your response. The assigned dietitian and counsellor stay in touch between updates for practical issues: a wedding, a trip, a food you cannot digest.
The weekly rhythm is the point: it catches small problems before they become reasons to quit, and it keeps the plan responsive. Most clients find the check-ins are what make the difference between a plan and a habit.

sections.heading: How is the plan personalised to Indian food?
sections.body:
The plans are built on everyday Indian food — dal, roti, rice, millets, sabzi, curd — portioned and timed around your routine. You are not asked to eat alien foods or shop at speciality stores.
Portions, oil, meal timing and pairings are adjusted to your goals, and festival and eating-out situations are planned for rather than forbidden. The test of the plan is a Tuesday evening, not a photo in an ad.

sections.heading: What do we not provide — and why?
sections.body:
We do not provide medicines, powders or supplements for weight loss, and we do not promise specific numbers. The site's FAQ is explicit: results vary with health history, lifestyle, medications and consistency.
This honesty is deliberate — sustainable weight management is built on food, activity and habits, not products, and anyone who guarantees weight loss while selling you something alongside is giving you a reason to be suspicious. You should know exactly what you are signing up for.

sections.heading: How do you decide if DietFiniti is right for you?
sections.body:
Book a consultation if you want a structured, personally adjusted plan with weekly support and honest expectations — and if you are ready to be an active participant. The program is a partnership: we bring the structure, you bring the consistency.
If you have a medical condition, we coordinate with your treating doctor — nutrition supports, not replaces, medical care. Ask us anything before starting; a good first conversation should answer your doubts, not create them.

faqs.question: How long is the DietFiniti program?
faqs.answer: Program duration depends on your goals and progress — most clients run 3–6 months with weekly reviews. Your dietitian sets milestones with you and adjusts the plan through the journey.

faqs.question: How much does the program cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the program and duration you choose. Contact DietFiniti directly for the current fee list — we do not publish outdated prices, and there are no hidden supplement charges.

faqs.question: Do you work with medical conditions?
faqs.answer: Yes — the history form captures your conditions and medications, and for diagnosed conditions we coordinate with your doctor. Nutrition guidance supports — it does not replace — medical care.

faqs.question: What results can I realistically expect?
faqs.answer: Weight loss typically averages 0.5–1kg per week for people who follow the plan, but results vary with history, lifestyle and consistency. We focus on sustainable habits and honest pace — no guaranteed numbers.

title: Online vs. Clinic Consultation: Which Is Right for You?
excerpt: DietFiniti offers consultations at the Mumbai and Thane clinics or fully online. Here's how they compare, what stays the same, and which fits your situation.
keywords: online dietitian consultation vs clinic, online nutritionist India, dietitian Mumbai clinic, which consultation type, virtual dietitian
author: Dietitian Tejal
quickAnswer: Online and clinic consultations deliver the same core: the history form, a personalised Indian-food plan, weekly reviews and ongoing support. Clinic visits add face-to-face interaction and are ideal if you prefer meeting in person or are nearby (Lower Parel or Thane); online consultations work anywhere in India with the same plan quality — most of our clients consult fully online. Choose by convenience and preference, not by quality — the plans are equal.

sections.heading: What stays the same in both formats?
sections.body:
Everything that matters: the detailed history form, the personalised plan built around Indian food and your routine, the assigned dietitian and counsellor, the weekly updates and plan adjustments, and the honest expectations about pace and results.
The assessment and follow-up work identically online — you answer the same questions, get the same planning, and message the same team. Your location changes the delivery method, not the plan.

sections.heading: Who is the clinic visit best for?
sections.body:
People in or near Mumbai (Lower Parel) and Thane who prefer face-to-face conversations, or who want to establish an in-person relationship with the team. A clinic visit can also be reassuring if you are new to dietitian care.
If you work near the clinic or pass it regularly, the visits can double as accountability checkpoints. The clinic is a real option — but it is an option, not a requirement.

sections.heading: Who is the online consultation best for?
sections.body:
Anyone outside Mumbai or Thane — the majority of our clients — plus people with busy schedules who do not want travel time, and those who simply prefer messaging over face-to-face meetings.
Online care is built around WhatsApp and calls: the same form, the same plan, the same weekly rhythm. For most people, the online format is not a compromise — it is the more practical version of the same service.

sections.heading: Does the plan quality differ between formats?
sections.body:
No — the plan is built from the same information and the same planning process regardless of how the consultation happens. A client in Pune and a client in Lower Parel with the same profile get the same standard of personalisation.
What differs is only the interaction: face-to-face versus messaging. Some people communicate better in person, some write better than they speak — choose the channel that suits you, knowing the substance is identical.

sections.heading: How do you choose?
sections.body:
Answer three questions: Where do I live? How much travel time am I willing to spend? Do I prefer talking in person or messaging? If the answer to the first is 'far from Lower Parel/Thane' or the second is 'little', go online — that is the majority choice.
And remember you can start online and visit later if you happen to be in the area — the formats are complementary, not competing. Either way, book the consultation that fits your week, because consistency is what makes any format work.

faqs.question: Is online consultation as effective as in-person?
faqs.answer: For nutrition planning and follow-up, yes — the assessment, plan and weekly support are the same. Research on telehealth nutrition shows comparable outcomes to in-person care for most conditions.

faqs.question: Can I switch between online and clinic visits?
faqs.answer: Yes — the formats are complementary. You can consult online most weeks and visit the clinic when convenient, or the reverse. The plan and support stay continuous either way.

faqs.question: What do I need for an online consultation?
faqs.answer: A phone or computer with WhatsApp or video calling, your health details, and 30–45 minutes of uninterrupted time for the first consultation. Everything else is handled by the team.

faqs.question: Can a family member join the online consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes — many clients involve family, especially when household meals and cooking need to change. The more the household understands the plan, the better it works.
